string-array.name: element_fact_descriptions
string-array.item: The most abundant element in the universe: it makes up about 75% of normal matter and powers the stars.
A noble gas lighter than air; it was first discovered in sunlight and years later on Earth.
The lightest metal of all: it is so low in density that it floats on water, even though it reacts with it.
A gray metal, very light and stiff; its dust is toxic if inhaled.
A dark, very hard metalloid; its most famous compound, borax, has been used for centuries.
The basis of all known life; depending on how its atoms are arranged, it can be soft graphite or diamond.
A colorless, odorless gas that makes up about 78% of the air you breathe.
A gas that makes up 21% of the air and is the most abundant element in the Earth\'s crust.
A pale yellow gas and the most reactive element of all: it reacts with almost any substance.
A noble gas that glows with an intense orange-red color when electricity passes through it.
A metal so soft it can be cut with a knife, and it reacts violently with water.
A light metal that burns with a very bright white light; it sits at the center of plants\' chlorophyll.
The most abundant metal in the Earth\'s crust; in the 19th century it was once worth more than gold.
A shiny gray metalloid; after oxygen, it is the most abundant element in the Earth\'s crust.
Its white form glows in the dark and ignites on its own in air; it is also part of your DNA and your bones.
A yellow solid found near volcanoes; some of its compounds smell like rotten eggs.
A toxic, yellowish-green gas; combined with sodium it becomes harmless table salt.
A noble gas that makes up almost 1% of the air; its name comes from the Greek for \'lazy\' because it hardly reacts.
A soft metal that burns in water with a lilac flame; your nerves and muscles need it to work.
A silvery, reactive metal; it is the most abundant mineral in your body, especially in bones and teeth.
A light, scarce metal whose existence Mendeleev predicted before it was discovered.
A metal as strong as many steels but much lighter, and very resistant to corrosion.
A hard, gray metal; its name comes from Vanadis, the Norse goddess of beauty, because of its colorful compounds.
A shiny, hard metal; small amounts give emerald its green and ruby its red.
A hard, brittle metal; plants and animals need it in small amounts.
The metal most used by humankind; it makes up a large part of the Earth\'s core.
A hard, magnetic metal; its compounds give glass and ceramics their intense cobalt blue.
A silvery, magnetic metal, very resistant to corrosion; it is plentiful in iron meteorites.
A reddish metal used for more than 10,000 years; over time it turns green, like the Statue of Liberty.
A bluish-gray metal; your body needs it for the immune system and for healing wounds.
A metal that melts in the palm of your hand: its melting point is only about 30 °C.
A shiny gray metalloid predicted by Mendeleev; it was key in the first transistors.
A gray metalloid famous as a poison in history and in mystery novels.
A nonmetal that conducts electricity better when light shines on it; its name comes from Selene, the Moon.
One of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature: dark red with a pungent smell.
A rare noble gas; its name means \'hidden\' in Greek, and no, it doesn\'t come from Superman\'s planet.
A very soft, reactive metal that ignites on its own on contact with air.
A soft, silvery metal that tints flames an intense red.
A silvery metal named after Ytterby, a Swedish village that gave its name to four elements.
A metal very resistant to corrosion; its oxide, cubic zirconia, imitates diamonds.
A soft gray metal that becomes a superconductor when cooled to extremely low temperatures.
A metal with one of the highest melting points (about 2600 °C); many enzymes need it.
The lightest element with no stable form; it was the first one created artificially, in 1937.
A hard, rare metal from the platinum family that barely corrodes.
One of the rarest and most expensive metals in the world; it is very shiny and reflective.
A silvery metal that can absorb hundreds of times its own volume of hydrogen.
The best conductor of electricity and heat of all the elements.
A soft, bluish and very toxic metal that builds up in the body.
A metal so soft that a fingernail can scratch it, and it creaks, like a tiny cry, when bent.
A silvery, malleable metal known since the Bronze Age; it also creaks when bent.
A shiny gray metalloid; in ancient Egypt its ore was used to line the eyes.
A rare, brittle metalloid; anyone who handles it can end up with garlic-smelling breath.
A shiny black solid that, when heated, turns directly into a violet vapor.
A heavy, rare noble gas that glows with a bluish-white light in discharge lamps.
A golden metal so soft that it melts at 28 °C and explodes on contact with water.
A silvery, reactive metal that turns flames green.
A soft, silvery metal that starts the lanthanide series, part of the so-called rare earths.
The most abundant rare earth; it gives off sparks when scraped.
A silvery rare-earth metal; its compounds have a lovely green color.
A rare-earth metal that forms the most powerful permanent magnets that exist.
A radioactive lanthanide almost nonexistent in nature; what is used is made in nuclear reactors.
A rare-earth metal named after samarskite, the mineral where it was found.
The most reactive rare earth; its name comes from Europe.
A rare-earth metal that is magnetic only below about 20 °C, nearly room temperature.
A silvery rare-earth metal, another of the elements named after the Swedish village of Ytterby.
Its name comes from the Greek for \'hard to get\', because isolating it took a lot of work.
It has one of the strongest atomic magnetisms; its name comes from Holmia, Latin for Stockholm.
A rare earth with pinkish compounds; it also owes its name to the Swedish village of Ytterby.
One of the least abundant rare earths; its name comes from Thule, an ancient name for northern Europe.
A soft, silvery rare-earth metal, the fourth element named after Ytterby.
The last of the lanthanides; its name comes from Lutetia, the ancient name of Paris.
A shiny metal that always appears alongside zirconium and is very hard to separate from it.
A bluish-gray metal highly resistant to corrosion; its name comes from Tantalus, a character in Greek mythology.
The metal with the highest melting point of all: about 3400 °C. It is also called wolfram.
One of the rarest elements in the Earth\'s crust and the last stable element to be discovered (1925).
The densest natural element: one liter of osmium would weigh more than 22 kg.
A metal highly resistant to corrosion; an iridium-rich layer marks the impact that wiped out the dinosaurs.
A precious metal, very dense and almost unalterable; it is rarer than gold.
A yellow metal that never tarnishes; it is formed in stellar explosions and collisions.
The only metal that is liquid at room temperature; it is silvery and its vapors are toxic.
A soft, highly toxic metal nicknamed \'the poisoner\'s poison\' because it has no taste or color.
A heavy, soft metal that the Romans used for pipes; it is toxic, especially for children.
A brittle metal that forms stair-stepped crystals with rainbow colors; it is barely toxic despite being so heavy.
A highly radioactive element discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie, named in honor of Poland, Marie\'s homeland.
One of the rarest naturally occurring elements: there is less than a gram of it in the whole Earth\'s crust at any one time.
A radioactive noble gas, invisible and odorless, that seeps out of some soils and can build up in basements.
Discovered in France in 1939; it is so unstable that there are only a few grams of it in the Earth\'s crust at any one time.
It glows faintly in the dark; the Curies discovered it, and it made ill the workers known as the \'Radium Girls\'.
A radioactive metal that glows with a pale blue light in the dark; it gives its name to the actinide series.
A radioactive metal about three times more abundant than uranium; its name comes from Thor, the Norse god of thunder.
A very rare and toxic radioactive metal; its name means \'before actinium\' because it turns into it.
A radioactive and very dense metal, named after the planet Uranus, which had been discovered only a few years earlier.
The first element heavier than uranium to be created (1940); it is named after Neptune, the planet after Uranus.
A radioactive metal named after Pluto; it changes shape and density with temperature like few other metals.
A synthetic element made in reactors; it is named after the Americas, just as europium is named after Europe.
A synthetic element named in honor of Marie and Pierre Curie; it glows in the dark because of its radioactivity.
A synthetic element created in 1949 in Berkeley, California, the city it is named after.
Created in 1950 at the University of California; a single microgram emits millions of neutrons per second.
It was discovered in 1952 in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb; its name honors Albert Einstein.
It also appeared in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb; its name honors Enrico Fermi.
It honors Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table; in 1955 only 17 atoms were made.
Named after Alfred Nobel; teams from Sweden, the United States and the Soviet Union disputed its discovery.
The last of the actinides, named after Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.
The first superheavy element after the actinides; it honors Ernest Rutherford, discoverer of the atomic nucleus.
Named after Dubna, the Russian city home to a famous nuclear physics laboratory.
It honors Glenn Seaborg, the first person to have an element named after him while still alive.
Created in Germany in 1981 and named after Niels Bohr, a pioneer of atomic physics.
Named after Hesse, the German state where it was first created in 1984.
It honors Lise Meitner, a physicist who helped explain nuclear fission; it was created in Germany in 1982.
Named after Darmstadt, the German city where it was created in 1994.
Named after Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays; it was created in Germany in 1994.
It honors Nicolaus Copernicus; calculations suggest it could be liquid at room temperature, like mercury.
The first element discovered in Asia: a Japanese team created it, and its name comes from Nihon, \'Japan\'.
Named after the Flerov Laboratory in Russia; it was expected to be more stable, but its atoms last seconds.
Created by Russian and American scientists; its name honors the Moscow region.
Named after the Lawrence Livermore Laboratory in California, which collaborated in its creation in Russia.
Its name comes from Tennessee: creating it required berkelium produced in that U.S. state.
The heaviest known element; it honors Yuri Oganessian, and only about five atoms have been detected.

string-array.name: element_fact_uses
string-array.item: Used to make ammonia for fertilizers, refine oil, and as a clean fuel in hydrogen fuel cells.
Inflates balloons, cools the magnets in MRI machines, and shields metal during welding.
It is the heart of batteries in phones, laptops, and electric cars; it is also used in psychiatric medicines.
Makes up the mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope and is used in springs, non-sparking tools, and aerospace parts.
Found in heat-resistant glass (borosilicate), fiberglass, detergents, and neodymium magnets.
Found in pencil lead, diamonds, steel, fuels, and carbon fiber.
Used in fertilizers, to preserve packaged food, and, as a liquid at -196 °C, to freeze samples.
Almost all living things breathe it; it is used in hospitals, in steelmaking, and in rockets.
The fluoride in toothpaste protects your teeth; it also forms the Teflon of nonstick pans.
It gives its name and color to classic neon signs; it is also used in some lasers.
Together with chlorine it forms table salt; its lamps give the yellow light of some street lighting.
Used in lightweight alloys for cars and laptops, in flares and fireworks, and as a supplement.
Found in soda cans, aluminum foil, windows, airplanes, and electrical cables; it also recycles very well.
It is the basis of computer and phone chips and of solar panels; as silica, it forms glass.
Used in fertilizers, in the striker strip for lighting matches, and in some detergents and colas.
Used to make sulfuric acid, to vulcanize the rubber in tires, in gunpowder, and in fungicides.
Disinfects drinking water and swimming pools, is found in bleaches, and is used to make PVC.
Fills incandescent bulbs, shields welds, and insulates the space between the panes of double-glazed windows.
Key in fertilizers (potash); you get it by eating bananas, potatoes, and beans.
Found in cement, lime, plaster, and chalk; also in milk and in bone supplements.
Small amounts strengthen the aluminum in bicycle frames, baseball bats, and airplane parts.
Used in airplanes, dental implants, and prostheses; its oxide is the white pigment in paints and sunscreens.
Hardens the steel of tools and springs; it is also used in flow batteries to store energy.
Gives chrome plating its shiny finish and keeps stainless steel from rusting.
Added to steel to make it stronger and found in ordinary alkaline batteries.
It is the basis of the steel in buildings, cars, and bridges; in your blood, hemoglobin uses it to carry oxygen.
Found in lithium batteries and in superalloys for jet turbines, and it is part of vitamin B12.
Used in stainless steel, in rechargeable batteries, and in many coins.
Found in almost all electrical wires, in pipes, and in alloys such as bronze and brass.
Protects steel from rusting (galvanizing) and is found in batteries, in brass, and in sunscreens.
With arsenic or nitrogen it forms LEDs, lasers, and high-frequency chips for phones.
Used in fiber optics, in lenses for infrared and night-vision cameras, and in satellite solar cells.
Forms the gallium arsenide in some chips and LEDs; it once protected wood, but today it is restricted because it is toxic.
Removes the greenish tint from glass, is found in anti-dandruff shampoos, and is an essential nutrient in small doses.
Used in fire retardants, in pool disinfectants, and in some medicines.
Used in some high-performance lamps, camera flashes, and insulating windows.
Used in compact atomic clocks, like those in some GPS satellites, and in research.
Gives fireworks and emergency flares their red; it is also used in ferrite magnets.
Used in white LEDs, medical lasers (YAG), and superconductors; it once supplied the red in tube TVs.
Coats the fuel in nuclear reactors and is used in dental crowns and ceramic knives.
It forms the superconducting magnets of MRI machines and the Large Hadron Collider, and it strengthens steel.
It hardens the steel used in tools, pipelines and engines; as a disulfide, it works as a lubricant.
One of its isotopes is used in millions of medical scans each year to look at bones, the heart and other organs.
It is used in electrical contacts, hard drives, as a catalyst, and to harden platinum.
It is in car catalytic converters to cut toxic gases, and it coats jewelry.
It is used in car catalytic converters, electronics, dentistry and white gold jewelry.
It is used in jewelry, coins, mirrors, electronic contacts and solar panels; also in antibacterial dressings.
It was used in nickel-cadmium batteries and yellow pigments; today it is in some thin-film solar panels.
Combined with tin (ITO), it lets touchscreens conduct electricity while staying transparent.
It is used in electronics solder, to coat steel cans (tinplate) and in bronze.
It is used as a fire retardant in plastics and fabrics, and to harden the lead in car batteries.
It is used in thin-film solar panels (cadmium telluride) and in thermoelectric devices.
It is added to table salt to protect the thyroid and is used as an antiseptic for wounds.
It is in car headlights, camera flashes and movie projectors; it is also an anesthetic and powers satellites with ion engines.
Its atomic clocks define the official second; it is also used in fluids for drilling oil wells.
It gives fireworks their green color; barium sulfate is swallowed to show the digestive system on X-rays.
It is used in high-quality camera lenses, in hybrid car batteries and in lighter flints.
It makes up lighter flints, polishes glass and lenses, and helps in catalytic converters.
It is used with neodymium in powerful magnets, in glassblowers\' goggles, and to give glass a yellow color.
Its magnets are in headphones, speakers, hard drives, electric car motors and wind turbines.
It has been used in glow-in-the-dark paint and in small nuclear batteries for pacemakers and spacecraft.
Its samarium-cobalt magnets withstand high temperatures; it is also used to relieve bone cancer pain.
It gives red and blue glow to screens and energy-saving bulbs, and its fluorescent ink protects euro banknotes.
It is injected as a contrast agent in MRI scans and absorbs neutrons in nuclear reactors.
It gives green color to screens and fluorescent bulbs, and is used in materials that change shape with a magnet.
It is added to neodymium magnets so they withstand heat in electric car motors and wind turbines.
It is used in medical lasers to break up kidney stones and in very powerful laboratory magnets.
It amplifies the signal in internet fiber optics, gives glass a pink color, and is used in dermatological lasers.
It is used in portable X-ray equipment and in medical and surgical lasers.
It is used in some of the most precise atomic clocks in the world and in industrial lasers.
It is used in PET scan detectors and, in radioactive form, in therapies against some cancers.
It absorbs neutrons in nuclear control rods and is part of modern processor chips.
Its tiny capacitors are in cell phones and computers; it is also used in surgical implants.
It forms the filament of classic light bulbs, the tiny balls in ballpoint pens, drill bits and cutting tools.
It is used in superalloys for jet engine turbines and as a catalyst to make high-octane gasoline.
It is used in fountain pen tips and electrical contacts, and its compounds stain samples for microscopes.
It is used in high-performance spark plugs, fountain pen tips and crucibles for growing crystals.
It is in catalytic converters, jewelry, electrodes, pacemakers and cancer drugs (cisplatin).
It is used in jewelry, coins and bank reserves, and in the contacts of cell phones and computers.
It was used in thermometers and barometers; it is still in some energy-saving bulbs, but its use is limited because it is toxic.
It is used in some heart imaging studies and in electronics; it was once used as rat poison.
It is found in car batteries and in the aprons that protect against X-rays; it is no longer used in gasoline.
It is the active ingredient in some stomach medicines and replaces lead in solders.
It is used in devices that remove static electricity in factories and was a heat source in some spacecraft.
It is used only in research, mainly to study cancer therapies with alpha particles.
It is measured in homes because of its health risk; it has been used in radiotherapy and to study groundwater.
It is used only in research, to study the structure of atoms with lasers.
It was once used in glow-in-the-dark watch paints; today one isotope is used to treat prostate cancer.
Actinium-225 is being studied in cancer therapies; it also serves as a neutron source in research.
It was used in gas lantern mantles and camera lenses; today it is being studied as a nuclear fuel.
It is used only in research, for example to date ocean sediments thousands of years old.
It is the fuel of nuclear power plants, which generate about 9% of the world\'s electricity.
It is used to produce plutonium-238 for spacecraft and in neutron detectors.
It is used in nuclear reactors and weapons; plutonium-238 powers probes such as the Voyagers and the Curiosity rover.
A tiny amount of americium-241 is in many household smoke detectors and helps save lives.
It is the alpha particle source in instruments on Mars rovers that analyze rocks.
It is used only in research, mainly as a target to make heavier elements, such as tennessine.
Its neutrons help start up nuclear reactors, search for oil and gold, and detect explosives.
It is used only in research: it has been produced in amounts so tiny that they can barely be seen.
It has no practical uses: it is the heaviest element that can be formed in a reactor and it is only studied.
It is used only in research, to understand how very heavy atoms behave.
It has no uses outside the lab; its atoms last from seconds to a little under an hour.
It exists only in laboratories, where it is made atom by atom to study its chemistry.
It is used only in research; its most stable form lasts just a few hours before decaying.
It is made a few atoms at a time and serves only to explore the limits of the periodic table.
It is used only in research; chemists have studied its compounds with just a handful of atoms.
Its atoms last seconds or, at most, about a minute; they serve only for basic science.
It is used only in research; with just a few atoms, scientists managed to study one of its oxides.
It has no practical uses: only a handful of atoms have been produced for research.
It exists for only a few seconds in the lab and is used to explore the physics of superheavy nuclei.
It is used only in research; chemically it is thought to resemble gold, but this has not yet been confirmed.
It is used only in research; with just a few atoms, it was shown to be very volatile.
It is used only in research; it took the Japanese team nine years to obtain three atoms.
It exists only in the lab, where scientists study whether it behaves like a metal or almost like a noble gas.
Its atoms last fractions of a second, so it is only useful for researching superheavy nuclei.
It has no practical use: a few dozen atoms that live for milliseconds have been observed.
It is used only in research: it is one of the newest elements and very few atoms are known.
It serves only science: each atom lasts less than a millisecond before decaying.
